title: Plant Taxonomy
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned 200L Plant Taxonomy curriculum: principles and history of classification, nomenclature rules, taxonomic hierarchy, herbarium methods, taxonomic evidence (morphological, cytological, chemical), and diagnostic features of major angiosperm families.

questions.question: Plant taxonomy is best defined as the branch of botany concerned with:
options: The identification, naming, and classification of plants
The internal structure of plant cells only
The physiological functions of plant organs
The genetic engineering of crop plants
questions.correct_answer: The identification, naming, and classification of plants
questions.explanation: Taxonomy encompasses three linked activities: identifying plants, giving them valid names, and arranging them into a classification system that reflects their relationships.

questions.question: The term 'systematics' differs from 'taxonomy' mainly in that systematics:
options: Additionally studies the evolutionary relationships and diversity among organisms
questions.correct_answer: Additionally studies the evolutionary relationships and diversity among organisms
questions.explanation: Systematics is the broader science of biological diversity and phylogenetic relationships, of which classification and nomenclature (taxonomy) form a part.

questions.question: The binomial system of nomenclature, in which every species is given a two-part Latin name, was formalised by:
questions.correct_answer: Carl Linnaeus
questions.explanation: Linnaeus established the consistent use of a genus name followed by a specific epithet in his 'Species Plantarum' (1753), the starting point for botanical nomenclature.

questions.question: In the binomial name Zea mays L., what does the abbreviation 'L.' represent?
options: The author who first validly published the name (Linnaeus)
The locality where the type specimen was collected
The family to which the plant belongs
questions.correct_answer: The author who first validly published the name (Linnaeus)
questions.explanation: An author citation follows the binomial to indicate who validly published that name; 'L.' is the standard abbreviation for Linnaeus.

questions.question: Botanical nomenclature is governed by rules set out in the:
options: International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi, and plants (ICN)
questions.correct_answer: International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi, and plants (ICN)
questions.explanation: The ICN (formerly ICBN) lays down the rules and recommendations for the formation and use of scientific names of plants, fungi and certain other organisms.

questions.question: The correct order of the standard taxonomic hierarchy from most inclusive to least inclusive is:
options: Kingdom, Division/Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species
Species, Genus, Family, Order, Class, Division, Kingdom
Kingdom, Family, Order, Class, Division, Genus, Species
Genus, Species, Family, Kingdom, Order, Class, Division
questions.correct_answer: Kingdom, Division/Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species
questions.explanation: The taxonomic ranks descend in inclusiveness from Kingdom down to Species, with each lower rank nested within the one above it.

questions.question: In plant family names, the standard suffix used is:
questions.correct_answer: -aceae
questions.explanation: Under the ICN, plant family names are formed by adding the suffix '-aceae' to the stem of a legitimate included genus name, e.g., Rosaceae from Rosa.

questions.question: The suffix conventionally used for plant order names is:
questions.correct_answer: -ales
questions.explanation: Plant order names take the standardised ending '-ales', for example Rosales, Fabales.

questions.question: A 'holotype' in botanical nomenclature refers to:
options: The single specimen designated by the author as the nomenclatural reference for a species name
Any specimen collected from the type locality
A specimen used only for DNA extraction
The most attractive specimen in a herbarium
questions.correct_answer: The single specimen designated by the author as the nomenclatural reference for a species name
questions.explanation: The holotype is the one specimen (or illustration) that the original author used or designated as the definitive reference point for applying the name.

questions.question: When the original holotype has been lost or destroyed, a new specimen chosen to serve as the standard reference is called a:
questions.correct_answer: Neotype
questions.explanation: A neotype is selected to replace a holotype that is missing or destroyed, so the name still has a clear nomenclatural reference point.

questions.question: A duplicate specimen collected from the same plant, at the same time, as the holotype is called an:
questions.correct_answer: Isotype
questions.explanation: An isotype is a duplicate of the holotype, part of the same gathering, often distributed to different herbaria.

questions.question: A dried, pressed, and labelled collection of plant specimens preserved for reference is called a(n):
questions.correct_answer: Herbarium
questions.explanation: A herbarium is a systematically arranged, preserved collection of plant specimens used for taxonomic identification, research, and reference.

questions.question: During herbarium preparation, freshly collected plant specimens are usually first:
options: Pressed and dried between absorbent sheets under weight or in a plant press
questions.correct_answer: Pressed and dried between absorbent sheets under weight or in a plant press
questions.explanation: Standard herbarium technique presses and dries specimens flat between blotting/newspaper sheets to preserve their form for mounting and long-term storage.

questions.question: A dichotomous key used for plant identification works by:
options: Presenting a series of paired, contrasting statements that lead the user to progressively narrow down the identity of a specimen
Grouping plants only by their common names
Requiring DNA sequencing at every step
questions.correct_answer: Presenting a series of paired, contrasting statements that lead the user to progressively narrow down the identity of a specimen
questions.explanation: A dichotomous key offers successive either/or choices of contrasting characters, each choice directing the user to the next couplet until an identification is reached.

questions.question: Numerical taxonomy differs from classical taxonomy mainly by:
options: Grouping organisms using quantitative analysis of many characters given equal weight, often with computer-based clustering
questions.correct_answer: Grouping organisms using quantitative analysis of many characters given equal weight, often with computer-based clustering
questions.explanation: Numerical (phenetic) taxonomy scores many characters and uses statistical/computational methods to calculate overall similarity, rather than weighting a few characters subjectively.

questions.question: Chemotaxonomy uses which type of evidence to classify plants?
options: Chemical constituents such as alkaloids, flavonoids, and other secondary metabolites
questions.correct_answer: Chemical constituents such as alkaloids, flavonoids, and other secondary metabolites
questions.explanation: Chemotaxonomy classifies and infers relationships among plants based on similarities and differences in their chemical compounds.

questions.question: Cytotaxonomy primarily uses which feature as evidence for classification?
questions.correct_answer: Chromosome number, size, and structure
questions.explanation: Cytotaxonomy applies karyological data, such as chromosome number and morphology, as taxonomic characters to assess relationships between taxa.

questions.question: A taxonomic group that includes an ancestor and ALL of its descendants is described as:
questions.correct_answer: Monophyletic
questions.explanation: A monophyletic group (clade) comprises a common ancestor and every one of its descendant taxa, which is the goal of cladistic classification.

questions.question: A group that includes a common ancestor and some, but not all, of its descendants is termed:
questions.correct_answer: Paraphyletic
questions.explanation: A paraphyletic group excludes one or more descendant lineages of the common ancestor, making it an incomplete evolutionary grouping, e.g., traditional 'Dicotyledons' excluding monocots.

questions.question: The modern classification system widely used for flowering plants, based largely on molecular phylogenetic (DNA sequence) data, is the:
questions.correct_answer: Angiosperm Phylogeny Group (APG) system
questions.explanation: The APG classification, developed from molecular phylogenetics, has largely replaced older morphology-based systems for classifying angiosperm orders and families.

questions.question: When two different scientific names have been given to the same taxon, the names are described as:
questions.correct_answer: Synonyms
questions.explanation: Synonyms are two or more names that apply to the same taxon; under nomenclatural priority, only one is treated as the correct (accepted) name.

questions.question: When the identical name has been applied to two different taxa by different authors, the names are:
questions.correct_answer: Homonyms
questions.explanation: Homonyms are identical names published for different taxa; the Code determines which usage (usually the earliest) is legitimate.

questions.question: The principle of nomenclatural priority states that:
options: The earliest validly published name for a taxon takes precedence over later names
The most commonly used name is always correct
Names given by the most senior scientist are preferred
Only Latin names published after 2000 are valid
questions.correct_answer: The earliest validly published name for a taxon takes precedence over later names
questions.explanation: Priority is a core principle of the ICN: among competing legitimate names for the same taxon, the earliest published name is generally accepted as correct.

questions.question: Members of the family Poaceae (grasses) are diagnostically characterised by:
options: Hollow, jointed stems (culms), narrow parallel-veined leaves with sheathing bases, and flowers reduced to florets in spikelets
Compound leaves with tendrils and papilionaceous flowers
Milky latex and a superior ovary of five fused carpels
Composite flower heads (capitula) of many small florets
questions.correct_answer: Hollow, jointed stems (culms), narrow parallel-veined leaves with sheathing bases, and flowers reduced to florets in spikelets
questions.explanation: Grasses have distinctive culms with nodes, leaves with parallel venation and sheathing bases, and highly reduced wind-pollinated flowers grouped into spikelets.

questions.question: The family Fabaceae (Leguminosae) is best recognised by its fruit type, the:
options: Legume (pod), which splits along two sutures
questions.correct_answer: Legume (pod), which splits along two sutures
questions.explanation: Fabaceae is characterised by the legume fruit, a dry dehiscent pod formed from a single carpel that opens along both sutures; many members also fix atmospheric nitrogen via root nodules.

questions.question: The family Asteraceae (Compositae) is distinguished by its inflorescence type, the:
options: Capitulum (composite head of many small florets on a common receptacle)
questions.correct_answer: Capitulum (composite head of many small florets on a common receptacle)
questions.explanation: Asteraceae flowers are condensed into a capitulum, a dense head of small ray and/or disc florets on a common receptacle, often surrounded by an involucre of bracts.

questions.question: A key diagnostic feature commonly used to distinguish monocotyledons from dicotyledons is:
options: Parallel leaf venation and floral parts typically in multiples of three in monocots, versus net (reticulate) venation and floral parts in multiples of four or five in dicots
Presence of chlorophyll only in monocots
questions.correct_answer: Parallel leaf venation and floral parts typically in multiples of three in monocots, versus net (reticulate) venation and floral parts in multiples of four or five in dicots
questions.explanation: Classic distinguishing features include venation pattern, floral merosity, number of cotyledons (one vs two), and vascular bundle arrangement in the stem.

questions.question: The family Euphorbiaceae is often recognised in the field by the presence of:
options: Milky latex in many members and a characteristic cyathium inflorescence in some genera (e.g. Euphorbia)
questions.correct_answer: Milky latex in many members and a characteristic cyathium inflorescence in some genera (e.g. Euphorbia)
questions.explanation: Many Euphorbiaceae species exude milky latex when cut, and the genus Euphorbia has a specialised cup-like inflorescence called a cyathium.

questions.question: In writing a floral formula, the symbol 'K' conventionally represents:
questions.correct_answer: Calyx (sepals)
questions.explanation: Standard floral formula notation uses K for calyx, C for corolla, A for androecium, and G for gynoecium.

questions.question: A superior ovary, as denoted in a floral formula and diagram, is one in which:
options: The ovary sits above the point of attachment of the other floral parts
The ovary sits below the other floral parts (hypogynous flower is impossible)
The ovary is fused to the petals only
questions.correct_answer: The ovary sits above the point of attachment of the other floral parts
questions.explanation: In a superior (hypogynous) ovary, the sepals, petals and stamens are attached below the ovary; a bar over the G number denotes this in a floral formula.

questions.question: The Solanaceae family, which includes tomato and pepper, typically has flowers with:
options: A radially symmetric (actinomorphic), five-lobed, fused corolla and five stamens alternating with the petals
A single fused perianth whorl of three parts only
questions.correct_answer: A radially symmetric (actinomorphic), five-lobed, fused corolla and five stamens alternating with the petals
questions.explanation: Solanaceae flowers are generally actinomorphic with a gamopetalous (fused) five-lobed corolla and five epipetalous stamens, a useful diagnostic combination.

questions.question: The species concept most commonly applied in practical plant taxonomy, defining a species by shared, consistent morphological characters distinguishing it from related taxa, is the:
questions.correct_answer: Morphological (taxonomic) species concept
questions.explanation: In practice, most plant taxonomists still delimit species primarily on consistent, diagnostic morphological differences, since interbreeding data (the biological species concept) is hard to obtain for most wild plants.

questions.question: An 'epithet' in a binomial such as Mangifera indica refers specifically to:
options: The second word, 'indica', which together with the genus name forms the full species name
questions.correct_answer: The second word, 'indica', which together with the genus name forms the full species name
questions.explanation: The specific epithet is the second element of a binomial; it has no independent taxonomic meaning apart from its combination with the genus name.

questions.question: The economically important family Malvaceae (which includes cotton and okra) is characterised by:
options: An epicalyx below the true calyx and numerous stamens fused into a staminal column (monadelphous androecium)
Naked seeds not enclosed in an ovary
Flowers reduced to florets within spikelets
questions.correct_answer: An epicalyx below the true calyx and numerous stamens fused into a staminal column (monadelphous androecium)
questions.explanation: Malvaceae is diagnosed by an epicalyx of bracteoles beneath the calyx and a distinctive monadelphous androecium in which the numerous stamen filaments are fused into a tube around the style.

questions.question: Which of these is a major practical use of herbarium specimens in taxonomy?
options: Serving as a permanent, verifiable reference for correctly identifying and naming plant material
Providing a source of fresh nectar for pollination studies
Replacing the need for field botanical surveys entirely
questions.correct_answer: Serving as a permanent, verifiable reference for correctly identifying and naming plant material
questions.explanation: Herbarium specimens document a plant's morphology at a fixed point and place, allowing later researchers to verify identifications, describe new taxa, and trace historical distributions.
